Queensland Fire Department via X Six large, shiny spheres washed up on a beach in northeastern Australia late last week, initially prompting alarm from authorities. On July 5, the Queensland Fire Department wrote on social media about the “discovery of several potentially hazardous objects.” Authorities established an exclusion zone, and over the weekend, members of the department collected “a number of the items,” per the statement. The fire department’s post features pictures of shiny, round, metallic-looking objects, each with two small protrusions at opposite ends. The odd spheres quickly led to humorous chatter among the residents of the little beach town. “Not much happens here. pages.text: Strange Stone Circles Hint at a Lost Nomadic Culture of the Sahara Desert | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE Strange Stone Circles Hint at a Lost Nomadic Culture of the Sahara Desert Long overshadowed by Egypt's pyramids and gold mines, the rugged Atbai Desert is finally revealing clues about the nomadic civilization that navigated its sand. Archaeologists have spotted 280 massive stone circles scattered across the Atbai Desert. The structures are likely tombs built by an ancient nomadic people who lived alongside Egypt’s pharaohs. Museo Castiglioni By Taylor Mitchell Brown Published August 11, 2026 Around 7,000 years ago, a string of severe droughts struck Egypt. The dry spells were part of an ongoing period of aridification that would continue for thousands of years, turning the once-green country into a sprawling desert. The transition drove many communities closer to the Nile, setting the stage for Egypt’s later pharaonic dynasties. But new research provides insight into a little-known nomadic population that refused to capitulate to the desert’s hostilities—and the mysterious traces they left behind. Earlier this year, researchers using satellite imagery reported discovering nearly 300 large stone circles scattered across the Atbai Desert, which sits in southern Egypt and northeastern Sudan between the Nile to the west and the Red Sea to the east. The structures, some of which measured over 200 feet across, provide clues about an early group of cattle herdsmen that preceded and then lived alongside Egypt’s great pyramids and pharaohs. Strategic Petroleum Reserve About the SPR The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), the world's largest supply of emergency crude oil was established primarily to reduce the impact of disruptions in supplies of petroleum products and to carry out obligations of the United States under the international energy program. The federally-owned oil stocks are stored in huge underground salt caverns at four sites along the coastline of the Gulf of America. The sheer size of the SPR (authorized storage capacity of 714 million barrels) makes it a significant deterrent to oil import cutoffs and a key tool in foreign policy. SPR oil is sold competitively when the President finds, pursuant to the conditions set forth in the Energy Policy and Conservation Act (EPCA), that a sale is required. Historically , the President has authorized emergency releases from the SPR on four occasions. Additionally, the Secretary of Energy may authorize limited releases in the form of exchanges with entities that are not part of the Federal Government. This authority allows the SPR to negotiate exchanges where the SPR ultimately receives more oil than it released; thereby acquiring additional oil. Strategies for the Control and Investigation of Mumps Outbreaks For Public Health Sept. 20, 2024 At a glance Mumps outbreak investigation and control generally consists of several steps, and some may occur in parallel. Public health officials can use this guidance and apply these tools when responding to mumps outbreaks in their jurisdiction. Why it's important Mumps outbreaks are a complex public health challenge and responses to these outbreaks can be resource intensive. Mumps cases have occurred in nearly every U.S. state each year since 2016. Outbreaks occur across many settings and range from 3 to >4,000 cases per outbreak. During many of these outbreaks, most cases have occurred in fully vaccinated people (2 MMR vaccine doses); limiting the impact of standard outbreak control measures for vaccine-preventable diseases. Effective and feasible control measures might differ by setting. During 2020–2022, there was a large reduction in mumps cases likely due to COVID-19 prevention measures, with 150–700 cases reported annually. Light pollution is disrupting nature, and a new study found artificial light even made tree leaves less appetizing to insects. Photograph by Jim Richardson, Nat Geo Image Collection By Olivia Ferrari Published August 5, 2024 Light pollution has increased about 10 percent each year over the past decade, making it one of the most drastic changes humans have made to the environment—and insects worldwide are noticing. Artificial lights that run all night, like streetlights, can make leaves grow tougher and less appetizing for insects, according to new research in Frontiers in Plant Science . This change to photosynthesis could threaten the small food chains that exist within cities. Conducted as part of activities supported through the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Partnership Contribution, the training aimed to strengthen national capacity for seasonal and pandemic influenza preparedness, with a focus on the role of seasonal influenza vaccine introduction as a platform for the potential deployment of pandemic vaccines during influenza epidemics and pandemics. pages.text: Striking Photos Reveal the Legacy of Yellowstone’s Wolves—30 Years After Their Return | National Geographic ANIMALS Striking Photos Reveal the Legacy of Yellowstone’s Wolves—30 Years After Their Return Three decades after the animals were reintroduced to the national park, revisit the legendary predators through National Geographic's archives. A yearling wolf from Yellowstone National Park’s Druid Peak pack in May 2008. Formed in 1996 from wolves brought from Canada, the pack became one of Yellowstone’s most famous, dominating the Lamar Valley and engaging in fierce rivalries with neighboring packs. At its peak in 2001, it numbered 37 wolves—the largest pack ever recorded in the park. Tom Murphy, National Geographic Image Collection By Jason Bittel Published November 6, 2026 Once eradicated by the government in the 1920s to protect livestock, gray wolves made a historic comeback in 1995 and 1996. In the three decades since, they’ve become some of North America’s most iconic—and controversial—wild animals. Some have become legends in their own right. There’s Wolf 8, a runt that eventually rose to leader status, and O-6, a formidable hunter known for taking down elk single-handedly. O-6 and her daughter, Spitfire, were both killed legally by hunters after wandering beyond the park’s borders. Whole packs have also become household names. For instance, Mollie’s Pack, originally known as the Crystal Creek Pack, descends from the first animals reintroduced to the park from Canada. pages.title: STS-114 - NASA
pages.description: STS-114 was the first Return to Flight mission since the tragic loss of Columbia Feb. 1, 2003. Two and a half years were spent researching and implementing safety improvements for orbiters and external tanks. They included greater in-depth examination of Reinforced Carbon-Carbon panels that are used on the wing leading edges, plus replacing bolts and new foam applications on the tanks.

pages.description: STS-73 marked second flight of U.S. Microgravity Laboratory (USML) and built on foundation of its predecessor, which flew on Columbia during Mission STS-50 in 1992. Research during USML-2 concentrated within same overall areas of USML-1, with many experiments flying for second time. Crew divided into two teams to work around the clock in 23-foot (seven-meter) long Spacelab module located in Columbia's payload bay.

Photograph: Rawpixel/Getty Images/iStockphoto Health Study of 100,000 Australians seeks causes of mental health disorders and early onset cancer Sax Institute is recruiting for 18 and Up, an intergenerational study of wellbeing and ageing that follows its landmark 45 and Up study Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jack Larkin Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.00 GMT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 09.48 GMT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Researchers hope to better understand the drivers of major health challenges facing younger people, such as mental illness and rising cancer rates, through the recruitment of 100,000 people for Australia’s largest intergenerational study of wellbeing and ageing. The independent and not-for-profit research institute the Sax Institute on Thursday launched the 18 and Up study, which will follow the health of those aged 18 to 90+ throughout their lives. Two decades ago, the institute started 45 and Up, now the largest population-based cohort study in the southern hemisphere, with more than 267,000 taking part ranging in age from 45 to older than 100.
